transcription.tex: Combine friction, resolving forces, \(F=ma\), inclined planes and connected particles. These preview examples are developed in the chapter.
\textbf{1. Equilibrium}\par Resolve forces to determine unknown magnitudes.
The supplied numerical sketch is inconsistent with equilibrium for \(g=9.8\); its arrows illustrate resolving forces.

\textbf{2. Weight and tension}\par A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle on a light string is held at \(30^\circ\) to the downward vertical by a force \(F\), \(30^\circ\) above horizontal. Find \(F\) and the tension. (8 marks)

\textbf{3. Inclined motion}\par A \(0.6\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle slides \(10\,\mathrm m\) down a rough \(25^\circ\) plane in \(3.5\,\mathrm s\), starting at \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find final speed, acceleration and friction coefficient. (3, 2, 5 marks)

\textbf{4. Connected particles}\par A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle on a rough \(30^\circ\) slope is connected by a taut light inextensible string over a smooth fixed pulley to a hanging \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle. With \(\mu=1/\sqrt3\), release from rest makes \(A\) move uphill. Find tension immediately after release. (9 marks)

transcription.tex: The particle is in equilibrium under the forces shown. Resolve horizontally and vertically to find the magnitudes \(P\) and \(Q\).
Resolve separately in the two directions, as before.

The resultant horizontal force is zero:\[P\cos30^\circ-4\cos45^\circ=0.\]Hence\[P\cos30^\circ=4\cos45^\circ.\]Vertically:\[P\sin30^\circ+4\sin45^\circ=Q.\]\[P=\frac{4\cos45^\circ}{\cos30^\circ}=3.27\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]\[Q=\frac{4\cos45^\circ}{\cos30^\circ}\sin30^\circ+4\sin45^\circ\]\[Q=4.46\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]

transcription.tex: The particle is in equilibrium on the inclined plane under the forces shown. Find \(P\) and \(\alpha\).
Use dotted, labelled arrows for resolved components. Blue arrows resolve P; green arrows resolve the weight.
Resolve the applied force:
Along the plane: \(P\cos\alpha\).
Normal to the plane: \(P\sin\alpha\).
Resolve the weight:
Into the plane: \(5\cos30^\circ\).
Down the plane: \(5\sin30^\circ\).

Along the plane:\[P\cos\alpha=8+5\sin30^\circ.\]Normal to it:\[P\sin\alpha+2=5\cos30^\circ.\]Divide the sine and cosine equations to eliminate \(P\), as in the \(R\sin(x+\alpha)\) method:\[\tan\alpha=\frac{5\cos30^\circ-2}{8+5\sin30^\circ}=0.222\ldots\]\[\alpha=12.5^\circ\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]\[P\sin\alpha=5\cos30^\circ-2\quad\Rightarrow\quad P=10.8\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]

transcription.tex: The particle is in equilibrium under the forces shown. Find \(Q\) and \(\beta\).
Along the plane:\[Q\cos\beta=5+6\sin30^\circ.\]Normal to it:\[Q\sin\beta+6\cos30^\circ=14.\]

\[Q\sin\beta=14-6\cos30^\circ,\quad Q\cos\beta=5+6\sin30^\circ.\]\[\tan\beta=\frac{14-6\cos30^\circ}{5+6\sin30^\circ}\]\[\beta=47.7^\circ\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]\[Q\cos\beta=5+6\sin30^\circ\quad\Rightarrow\quad Q=11.9\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]

transcription.tex: 2. For each particle in static equilibrium:\par i. Draw a triangle of forces.\par ii. Use trigonometry to find unknown forces \(P,Q\) and unknown angle \(\theta\).
a.

Horizontally, \(Q-P\cos60^\circ=0\). (1)\par Vertically, \(P\sin60^\circ-4\sqrt3=0\). (2)\[P=\frac{4\sqrt3}{\sin60^\circ}=4\sqrt3\frac2{\sqrt3}=8\,\mathrm N.\]Substitute into (1):\[Q=8\cos60^\circ=8\times\tfrac12=4\,\mathrm N.\]
b.

Horizontally:\[4\cos45^\circ+P\cos\theta-7=0\]\[P\cos\theta=7-4\cos45^\circ.\qquad(1)\]Vertically:\[4\sin45^\circ-P\sin\theta=0\]\[P\sin\theta=4\sin45^\circ.\qquad(2)\]Divide (2) by (1):\[\tan\theta=\frac{4\sin45^\circ}{7-4\cos45^\circ}=\frac{2.828\ldots}{4.172\ldots}=0.678\ldots\]\[\theta=34.1^\circ\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]Substitute into (2), using full precision:\[P=\frac{2.828\ldots}{\sin\theta}=5.04\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]

transcription.tex: 3. Each particle rests in equilibrium on the plane under the forces shown. Find \(P\) and \(Q\).
a.
Normal to the plane:\[P=5\cos30^\circ=4.33\,\mathrm N.\]Along the plane:\[Q=5\sin30^\circ=2.5\,\mathrm N.\]
b.

Along the plane:\[Q-10\sin45^\circ=0.\qquad(1)\]Normal to it:\[P-10\cos45^\circ=0.\qquad(2)\]\[P=10\cos45^\circ=5\sqrt2=7.07\,\mathrm N.\]\[Q=10\sin45^\circ=5\sqrt2=7.07\,\mathrm N.\]Both answers to 3 s.f.

transcription.tex: Along the plane:\[Q+2\cos60^\circ-6\sin60^\circ=0.\]Normal to it:\[P-2\sin60^\circ-6\cos60^\circ=0.\]\[P=2\sin60^\circ+6\cos60^\circ\]\[P=4.73\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]\[Q=6\sin60^\circ-2\cos60^\circ\]\[Q=4.20\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]

Along the plane:\[8\cos45^\circ-10\sin30^\circ-Q=0.\]Normal to it:\[P+8\sin45^\circ-10\cos30^\circ=0.\]\[P=10\cos30^\circ-8\sin45^\circ\]\[=5\sqrt3-4\sqrt2=3.00\,\mathrm N.\]\[Q=8\cos45^\circ-10\sin30^\circ\]\[=4\sqrt2-5=0.657\,\mathrm N.\]Both to 3 s.f.

Down the plane:\[8\sin30^\circ-Q\cos30^\circ=0.\]Normal to it:\[P-Q\sin30^\circ-8\cos30^\circ=0.\]\[Q=\frac{8\sin30^\circ}{\cos30^\circ}=8\tan30^\circ\]\[=\frac{8\sqrt3}{3}=4.62\,\mathrm N.\]\[P=Q\sin30^\circ+8\cos30^\circ\]\[=\frac{8\sqrt3}{3}\frac12+8\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\]\[=\frac{4\sqrt3}{3}+4\sqrt3=\frac{16\sqrt3}{3}\]\[P=9.24\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]

transcription.tex: \textbf{Challenge}\par Three coplanar forces of magnitudes \(A,B,C\) act on a particle in equilibrium, as shown. Prove\[\frac A{\sin\alpha}=\frac B{\sin\beta}=\frac C{\sin\gamma}.\]
Extend each line of action backwards through the particle to identify supplementary angles between the lines.
Equilibrium means the force vectors form a closed triangle.

By the sine rule:\[\frac A{\sin(180^\circ-\alpha)}=\frac B{\sin(180^\circ-\beta)}\]\[=\frac C{\sin(180^\circ-\gamma)}.\]For any angle \(\theta\), \(\sin(180^\circ-\theta)=\sin\theta\). Hence\[\frac A{\sin\alpha}=\frac B{\sin\beta}=\frac C{\sin\gamma}.\]

transcription.tex: Apply resolving to tension, weight and pulleys. A smooth bead \(Y\) is threaded on a light inextensible string whose ends are fixed at \(X,Z\), at the same horizontal level. A horizontal \(8\,\mathrm N\) force parallel to \(ZX\) holds the bead in equilibrium, with \(Y\) vertically below \(X\) and \(\angle XZY=30^\circ\). Find the tension and the bead’s weight.
Draw the force diagram.
The smooth bead allows the tension to be the same in both parts of the light string.
Horizontally:\[T\cos30^\circ=8\quad\Rightarrow\quad T=9.24\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]
Vertically:\[W=T+T\sin30^\circ=13.9\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]Use the unrounded value of \(T\).

transcription.tex: A \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) mass rests on a smooth plane at \(45^\circ\) to horizontal. A cable runs up the line of greatest slope over a smooth pulley and supports a freely hanging \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) mass. Model the masses as particles and the cable as a light inextensible string. A horizontal force \(P\) acts towards the plane on the \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) mass; the system is in equilibrium. Find: (a) \(P\); (b) the normal reaction; (c) how the smooth-pulley assumption is used.
Draw the force diagram.
For the \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) mass, vertically:\[T=g.\]
For the \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) mass, up the plane:\[T+P\cos45^\circ=3g\sin45^\circ.\]\[P=\frac{3g\sin45^\circ-g}{\cos45^\circ}\]\[=3g-g\sqrt2=16\,\mathrm N\quad(2\text{ s.f.}).\]
Normal to the plane:\[R=3g\cos45^\circ+P\sin45^\circ\]\[=6g\frac{\sqrt2}2-g=32\,\mathrm N\quad(2\text{ s.f.}).\]
The pulley is smooth, so the tension is the same on both sides of it.

transcription.tex: Edexcel M1 (Old), May 2013(R), Q2\par A particle of weight \(8\,\mathrm N\) is attached at \(C\) to two light inextensible strings \(AC,BC\). Their other ends are fixed to a horizontal ceiling at \(A,B\). The particle rests in equilibrium; the strings lie in a vertical plane, at \(35^\circ\) and \(25^\circ\) to horizontal respectively. Find (i) the tension in \(AC\); (ii) the tension in \(BC\).
The particle cannot slide along the string: these are two separate strings with separate tensions. Introduce \(T_A,T_B\).

Resolve horizontally:\[T_A\cos35^\circ=T_B\cos25^\circ.\]Resolve vertically:\[T_A\sin35^\circ+T_B\sin25^\circ=8.\]Eliminate one unknown:\[T_B\frac{\cos25^\circ}{\cos35^\circ}\sin35^\circ+T_B\sin25^\circ=8,\]or\[T_A\sin35^\circ+T_A\frac{\cos35^\circ}{\cos25^\circ}\sin25^\circ=8.\]\[T_A=8.37\,\mathrm N,\qquad T_B=7.57\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]

transcription.tex: 5. A smooth bead \(B\) is threaded on a light inextensible string fixed at \(A,C\), at the same horizontal level. A horizontal \(2\,\mathrm N\) force parallel to \(CA\) holds it in equilibrium. The string sections make angles \(60^\circ,30^\circ\) with horizontal. Find (a) the tension; (b) the bead’s mass; (c) state how the smooth-bead assumption is used.

Let the tension be \(T\) and mass be \(m\). Resolve horizontally:\[T\cos30^\circ-T\cos60^\circ-2=0\]\[T(\cos30^\circ-\cos60^\circ)=2\]\[T=\frac2{\cos30^\circ-\cos60^\circ}\]\[=5.46\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]

Vertically:\[T\sin60^\circ+T\sin30^\circ-mg=0\]\[mg=T(\sin60^\circ+\sin30^\circ)\]\[m=\frac2g(\sqrt3+1)\left(\frac{\sqrt3}2+\frac12\right)\]\[=\frac{4+2\sqrt3}g=0.76\,\mathrm{kg}\quad(2\text{ s.f.}).\]
A smooth bead has no friction with the string, so the tension is the same in both sections.

transcription.tex: 6. A smooth bead \(B\) is threaded on a light inextensible string fixed at \(A,C\), where \(A\) is vertically above \(C\). A horizontal \(2\,\mathrm N\) force holds the bead in equilibrium. Sections \(AB,BC\) make angles \(30^\circ,60^\circ\) with vertical respectively. Find (a) the tension; (b) the bead’s mass, to the nearest gram.

Let tension be \(T\) and mass be \(m\). Horizontally:\[2-T\cos60^\circ-T\cos30^\circ=0\]\[T(\cos60^\circ+\cos30^\circ)=2\]\[T=\frac2{\cos60^\circ+\cos30^\circ}\]\[=1.46\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]
Vertically:\[T\sin60^\circ-T\sin30^\circ-mg=0.\]\[m=\frac{4-2\sqrt3}g\]\[=0.05468\ldots\,\mathrm{kg}\]\[=55\,\mathrm g\quad\text{to the nearest gram}.\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: 7. A particle of weight \(2\,\mathrm N\) rests on a smooth horizontal surface in equilibrium under the two external forces shown. One is a horizontal \(1\,\mathrm N\) force; the other has magnitude \(P\), at angle \(\theta\) to horizontal, where \(\tan\theta=12/5\). Find (a) \(P\); (b) the normal reaction.

\[\tan\theta=\frac{12}5\]\[\Rightarrow\quad\sin\theta=\frac{12}{13},\quad\cos\theta=\frac5{13}.\]Let the normal reaction be \(R\). Horizontally:\[P\cos\theta-1=0\]\[P=\frac1{\cos\theta}=\frac{13}5=2.6\,\mathrm N.\]
Vertically:\[R-P\sin\theta-2=0\]\[R=P\sin\theta+2\]\[=2.6\times\frac{12}{13}+2\]\[=2.4+2=4.4\,\mathrm N.\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: 11. Particle \(A\), mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\), rests in equilibrium on a smooth plane at angle \(\theta\) to horizontal, where \(\tan\theta=3/4\). A light inextensible string runs from \(A\) over a smooth pulley to hanging particle \(B\), mass \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\). A force \(F\) acts on \(A\) down the line of greatest slope. Find (a) the normal reaction; (b) \(F\); (c) state how the smooth-pulley assumption is used.

Let the normal reaction be \(R\), tension \(T\). For the \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) mass:\[T-5g=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad T=5g.\]For the \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) mass, normal to plane:\[R-2g\cos\theta=0\]\[R=2g\times\frac45=16\,\mathrm N\quad(2\text{ s.f.}).\]
Up the plane:\[T-F-2g\sin\theta=0\]\[F=T-2g\sin\theta=5g-2g\times\frac35\]\[=\frac{19g}5=37\,\mathrm N\quad(2\text{ s.f.}).\]
A smooth pulley has no friction with the string, so the tension is the same on each side.

transcription.tex: 12. A particle of weight \(20\,\mathrm N\) rests in equilibrium on a smooth \(45^\circ\) inclined plane. A horizontal \(5\,\mathrm N\) force acts to the left; force \(P\) acts at \(30^\circ\) above the plane. Find the normal reaction.

Let the normal reaction be \(R\). Resolve along the plane first: \(P\) is the only unknown in that direction.\[P\cos30^\circ-5\cos45^\circ-20\sin45^\circ=0\]\[P=\frac{5\cos45^\circ+20\sin45^\circ}{\cos30^\circ}\]\[=20.4\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]Normal to the plane:\[R+P\sin30^\circ+5\sin45^\circ-20\cos45^\circ=0\]\[R=20\cos45^\circ-5\sin45^\circ-P\sin30^\circ\]\[=0.400\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]Use unrounded \(P\).

transcription.tex: Friction satisfies \(F\leq\mu R\), with \(F=\mu R\) in limiting equilibrium or sliding under this model. At rest, friction opposes the motion that would occur without it.\par A \(10\,\mathrm{kg}\) box rests in limiting equilibrium on a rough plane at \(20^\circ\) above horizontal. (a) Find \(\mu\). A horizontal force \(P\) is then applied towards the plane. (b) Find the maximum \(P\) for equilibrium.
Normal to plane:\[R=10g\cos20^\circ.\]Up the plane:\[\mu R=10g\sin20^\circ.\]\[\mu=\frac{10g\sin20^\circ}{10g\cos20^\circ}=\tan20^\circ\]\[=0.36\quad(2\text{ s.f.}).\]

At maximum \(P\), impending motion is uphill, so friction acts downhill.\[R=10g\cos20^\circ+P\sin20^\circ\]\[P\cos20^\circ=10g\sin20^\circ+\mu R\]\[P\cos20^\circ=10g\sin20^\circ\]\[{}+\tan20^\circ(10g\cos20^\circ+P\sin20^\circ).\]Collect terms:\[P=\frac{20g\sin20^\circ}{\cos20^\circ-\tan20^\circ\sin20^\circ}\]\[=82\,\mathrm N\quad(2\text{ s.f.}).\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: Edexcel M1 (Old), January 2006, Q5\par A parcel of weight \(10\,\mathrm N\) lies on a rough \(30^\circ\) inclined plane. Horizontal force \(P\) acts towards the plane. It is in equilibrium on the point of slipping uphill; the normal reaction is \(18\,\mathrm N\), coefficient of friction \(\mu\). Find (a) \(P\) (4 marks); (b) \(\mu\) (5 marks). The horizontal force is removed. (c) Determine whether the parcel moves (5 marks).
Normal to plane:\[P\sin30^\circ+10\cos30^\circ=18\]\[P=18.7\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]
Parallel to plane:\[P\cos30^\circ=10\sin30^\circ+F.\]\[F=18\mu.\]\[\mu=\frac{P\cos30^\circ-10\sin30^\circ}{18}\]\[=0.621\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]Use unrounded \(P\).

Now \(R_{\rm new}=10\cos30^\circ\). The weight component downhill is\[10\sin30^\circ=5\,\mathrm N.\]Maximum available friction:\[F_{\max}=\mu R_{\rm new}=5.37\,\mathrm N.\]Since \(5.37>5\), friction can balance the weight component: the parcel does not slide.

transcription.tex: 8. A horizontal \(20\,\mathrm N\) force acts on a \(1.5\,\mathrm{kg}\) block resting in equilibrium on a rough \(30^\circ\) plane. The force acts in the vertical plane containing the line of greatest slope. Find (a) the normal reaction; (b) the friction magnitude and direction; (c) the minimum coefficient of friction.

Let the normal reaction be \(R\) and friction \(F\) act downhill. Normal to the plane:\[R-20\sin30^\circ-1.5g\cos30^\circ=0\]\[R=20\sin30^\circ+1.5g\cos30^\circ\]\[=22.7\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]Parallel to it:\[20\cos30^\circ-F-1.5g\sin30^\circ=0\]\[F=20\cos30^\circ-1.5g\sin30^\circ\]\[=9.97\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}),\text{ downhill}.\]

The minimum \(\mu\) occurs when required friction equals \(\mu R\):\[F=\mu R\]\[9.9705\ldots=\mu\times22.730\ldots\]\[\mu=\frac{9.9705\ldots}{22.730\ldots}=0.43863\ldots\]The coefficient must be at least \(0.439\) (3 s.f.) to prevent sliding.

transcription.tex: 9. A \(3\,\mathrm{kg}\) box lies on a rough plane inclined at \(40^\circ\) to horizontal. A horizontal force \(X\) holds it in equilibrium, acting in the vertical plane containing the line of greatest slope. The coefficient of friction is \(0.3\); the box is in limiting equilibrium about to move uphill. Find (a) \(X\); (b) the normal reaction.

Normal to plane:\[R-X\sin40^\circ-3g\cos40^\circ=0\]\[R=X\sin40^\circ+3g\cos40^\circ.\quad(1)\]Parallel to plane:\[X\cos40^\circ-F-3g\sin40^\circ=0\]\[F=X\cos40^\circ-3g\sin40^\circ.\quad(2)\]Limiting friction: \(F=\mu R\). Substitute (1),(2):\[X\cos40^\circ-3g\sin40^\circ\]\[=0.3(X\sin40^\circ+3g\cos40^\circ).\]

\[X\cos40^\circ-0.3X\sin40^\circ\]\[=0.9g\cos40^\circ+3g\sin40^\circ\]\[X(\cos40^\circ-0.3\sin40^\circ)\]\[=0.9g\cos40^\circ+3g\sin40^\circ\]\[X=\frac{0.9g\cos40^\circ+3g\sin40^\circ}{\cos40^\circ-0.3\sin40^\circ}\]\[=\frac{25.65\ldots}{0.5732\ldots}=44.8\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]
Substitute the unrounded \(X\) in (1):\[R=X\sin40^\circ+3g\cos40^\circ\]\[=51.3\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: 11. A \(0.5\,\mathrm{kg}\) box lies on a \(40^\circ\) inclined plane with coefficient of friction \(1/5\). A light string keeps it in equilibrium, lying in the vertical plane containing the line of greatest slope, at \(20^\circ\) above the plane. Model the box as a particle. The tension is \(T\). Find its possible range, with limiting equilibrium at the endpoints.

Normal to the plane:\[R-0.5g\cos40^\circ+T\sin20^\circ=0\]\[R=0.5g\cos40^\circ-T\sin20^\circ.\]At \(T_{\max}\), impending motion is uphill and \(F=\mu R\) acts downhill:\[T_{\max}\cos20^\circ-0.5g\sin40^\circ\]\[=F\]\[T_{\max}\cos20^\circ-0.5g\sin40^\circ\]\[{}-\tfrac15\bigl(0.5g\cos40^\circ\bigr)\]\[{}+\tfrac15T_{\max}\sin20^\circ=0\]\[T_{\max}=\frac{0.5g\sin40^\circ+0.1g\cos40^\circ}{\cos20^\circ+0.2\sin20^\circ}\]\[=3.8690\ldots\,\mathrm N.\]

At \(T_{\min}\), impending motion is downhill and \(F=\mu R\) acts uphill:\[T_{\min}\cos20^\circ-0.5g\sin40^\circ\]\[=-F\]\[T_{\min}\cos20^\circ-0.5g\sin40^\circ\]\[{}+\tfrac15\bigl(0.5g\cos40^\circ\bigr)\]\[{}-\tfrac15T_{\min}\sin20^\circ=0\]\[T_{\min}=\frac{0.5g\sin40^\circ-0.1g\cos40^\circ}{\cos20^\circ-0.2\sin20^\circ}\]\[=2.7533\ldots\,\mathrm N.\]Thus \(2.75\leq T\leq3.87\,\mathrm N\), with endpoints rounded to 3 s.f.

transcription.tex: 12. A \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) box lies on a plane at \(40^\circ\) to horizontal. A light string, at \(20^\circ\) above the plane in the vertical plane containing its line of greatest slope, holds the box in equilibrium on the point of moving uphill. Model it as a particle. The tension is \(10\,\mathrm N\). Find the coefficient of friction \(\mu\).

Normal to the plane:\[R+10\sin20^\circ-g\cos40^\circ=0\]\[R=g\cos40^\circ-10\sin20^\circ=4.087\ldots\,\mathrm N.\]Parallel to the plane:\[10\cos20^\circ-F-g\sin40^\circ=0\]\[F=10\cos20^\circ-g\sin40^\circ=3.0976\ldots\,\mathrm N.\]Friction is limiting, \(F=\mu R\):\[\mu=\frac FR=\frac{3.0976\ldots}{4.087\ldots}=0.758\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: 13. A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle rests in limiting equilibrium on a rough plane at angle \(\theta\) above horizontal, where \(\tan\theta=3/4\). A horizontal force \(P\), directed into the plane, is then applied. Given that the particle remains in equilibrium, find the maximum possible \(P\).

\[\tan\theta=\frac34\Rightarrow\sin\theta=\frac35,\quad\cos\theta=\frac45.\]Before \(P\) is applied, impending motion is downhill; limiting friction acts uphill.\[R=2g\cos\theta\]\[2g\sin\theta=F_{\max}=\mu R=\mu\times2g\cos\theta\]\[\mu=\tan\theta=\frac34.\]

At maximum \(P\), impending motion is uphill, so friction acts downhill.\[R^{\prime}=2g\cos\theta+P\sin\theta\]\[P\cos\theta=F_{\max}+2g\sin\theta\]\[P\cos\theta=\mu R^{\prime}+2g\sin\theta\]\[P\cos\theta=\mu(2g\cos\theta+P\sin\theta)+2g\sin\theta\]\[P(\cos\theta-\mu\sin\theta)=2g(\mu\cos\theta+\sin\theta)\]\[P\left(\frac45-\frac34\times\frac35\right)=2\times9.8\left(\frac34\times\frac45+\frac35\right)\]\[0.35P=23.52\quad\Rightarrow\quad P=67.2\,\mathrm N.\]The maximum is \(67.2\,\mathrm N\).

transcription.tex: For a stationary rigid body:\par • The resultant force is zero.\par • The resultant moment is zero.\par These are the moment problems already studied, now including friction.\par A uniform rod \(AB\), mass \(40\,\mathrm{kg}\), length \(10\,\mathrm m\), has end \(A\) on rough horizontal ground and rests against a smooth peg \(C\), where \(AC=8\,\mathrm m\). It is in limiting equilibrium at \(15^\circ\) to horizontal. Find (a) the reaction at \(C\); (b) the ground’s coefficient of friction.
The frictional force prevents the rod from sliding along the ground.
a. Take moments about A.
\[40g\times5\cos15^\circ=N\times8\]\[N=236.65\ldots\,\mathrm N.\]The reaction at \(C\) has magnitude \(240\,\mathrm N\) (2 s.f.).
b. Resolve horizontally, then vertically.
\[\mu R=N\sin15^\circ=61.25\,\mathrm N\]
\[R+N\cos15^\circ=40g\]\[R=40g-N\cos15^\circ=163.41\ldots\,\mathrm N\]\[\mu=\frac{61.25}{163.41\ldots}=0.37\quad(2\text{ s.f.}).\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: A ladder \(AB\), mass \(m\), length \(3a\), rests with \(A\) on rough horizontal ground and \(B\) against a smooth vertical wall. A load of mass \(2m\) is fixed at \(C\), where \(AC=a\). Model the ladder as a uniform rod in a vertical plane perpendicular to the wall, and the load as a particle. The ladder rests in limiting equilibrium at \(60^\circ\) to the ground. (a) Find the coefficient of friction with the ground. (b) State how the uniform-ladder assumption is used.
Two different reaction forces need different variables.
Horizontally:\[\mu R=P.\]
Vertically:\[R=2mg+mg=3mg.\]

Take moments about \(B\):\[2mg\times2a\cos60^\circ+mg\times1.5a\cos60^\circ\]\[{}+\mu R\times3a\sin60^\circ=R\times3a\cos60^\circ.\]Divide by \(a\):\[2.75mg+\frac{3\sqrt3}2\mu R=1.5R.\]Substitute \(R=3mg\):\[2.75mg+\frac{3\sqrt3}2\mu(3mg)=1.5(3mg)\]\[2.75+\frac{9\sqrt3}2\mu=4.5\]\[\mu=0.225\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]
The ladder’s weight acts at its midpoint.

transcription.tex: 4. A uniform ladder, mass \(20\,\mathrm{kg}\), length \(8\,\mathrm m\), rests against a smooth vertical wall with its lower end on rough horizontal ground. The ground’s coefficient of friction is \(0.3\); the ladder makes angle \(\theta\) with horizontal, where \(\tan\theta=2\). A \(30\,\mathrm{kg}\) boy climbs it. Model the ladder as a uniform rod and the boy as a particle. (a) How far can he climb before slipping occurs? (b) Criticise the model for (i) the ladder, (ii) the wall.

Suppose the boy reaches \(B\), distance \(x\) from the foot \(A\), while the ladder remains in contact with the ground.\[F=N,\qquad R=50g.\]Moments about \(A\):\[20g\times4\cos\theta+30g\times x\cos\theta\]\[=N\times8\sin\theta\]\[80g+30gx=8N\tan\theta\]\[N=F=\mu R=\frac{80g+30gx}{16}.\]\[\text{Here }\tan\theta=2.\]\[0.3\times50g=\frac{80g+30gx}{16}\]\[240=80+30x\quad\Rightarrow\quad x=5\tfrac13\,\mathrm m.\]
The ladder may not be uniform.
There may be friction between the ladder and wall.

transcription.tex: 8. A uniform ladder rests in limiting equilibrium with one end on rough horizontal ground and the other against a rough vertical wall. The coefficients of friction are \(\mu_1\) at the ground and \(\mu_2\) at the wall. It makes angle \(\theta\) with horizontal. Show\[\tan\theta=\frac{1-\mu_1\mu_2}{2\mu_1}.\]

Let \(R,F\) be the ground’s normal reaction and friction; \(S,G\) the wall’s reaction and friction; and \(X\) the intersection of the lines of action of \(R,S\). Let length be \(2a\), weight \(W\). Limiting friction gives\[F=\mu_1R,\qquad G=\mu_2S.\]

Take moments about \(X\):\[Wa\cos\theta=F\times2a\sin\theta+G\times2a\cos\theta\]\[W=2F\tan\theta+2G.\qquad(1)\]Horizontally, \(F=S\); vertically, \(W=R+G\). Substitute for \(W,F\) in (1):\[R+G=2\mu_1R\tan\theta+2G\]\[R-G=2\mu_1R\tan\theta\]\[R-\mu_1\mu_2R=2\mu_1R\tan\theta\]\[\frac{1-\mu_1\mu_2}{2\mu_1}=\tan\theta.\]

transcription.tex: 9. A uniform ladder of weight \(W\) rests in equilibrium on rough horizontal ground against a smooth vertical wall. Its vertical plane is perpendicular to the wall; the ladder makes \(60^\circ\) with horizontal. The ground’s coefficient of friction is \(\mu\). (a) Find the wall force in terms of \(W\). (b) Show that \(\mu\geq\sqrt3/6\).

Let the ends be \(A,B\), wall reaction \(P\), ground reaction \(R\), ground friction \(F\), and length \(2a\). Take moments about \(A\):\[W\times a\cos60^\circ=P\times2a\cos30^\circ\]\[P=\frac{Wa\cos60^\circ}{2a\cos30^\circ}=\frac W{2\sqrt3}.\qquad(1)\]

Vertically, \(R=W\). (2)\par Horizontally, \(F=P\). (3)\par Equilibrium requires \(F\leq\mu R\), hence\[P\leq\mu R\quad\text{by (3)},\]\[\frac W{2\sqrt3}\leq\mu R\quad\text{by (1)},\]\[\frac W{2\sqrt3}\leq\mu W\quad\text{by (2)}.\]Therefore\[\mu\geq\frac{\sqrt3}6.\]

transcription.tex: 10. A uniform rod \(XY\), weight \(20\,\mathrm N\), length \(90\,\mathrm{cm}\), rests on two parallel pegs with \(X\) above \(Y\), in a vertical plane perpendicular to the peg axes. It makes \(30^\circ\) with horizontal and touches the pegs at \(P,Q\), where \(XP=20\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(XQ=60\,\mathrm{cm}\). (a) Find the normal force components at \(P,Q\). The friction coefficient at each peg is \(\mu\). (b) Given impending slip, find \(\mu\).

Let \(T,G\) be the normal and friction forces at \(P\); \(S,F\) those at \(Q\). Moments about \(P\):\[S\times40=20\times25\cos30^\circ\]\[S=\frac{20\times25\times\sqrt3/2}{40}=\frac{25\sqrt3}4\,\mathrm N.\]Moments about \(Q\):\[T\times40=20\times15\cos30^\circ\]\[T=\frac{20\times15\times\sqrt3/2}{40}=\frac{15\sqrt3}4\,\mathrm N.\]

Along the rod:\[G+F=20\cos60^\circ=10.\qquad(1)\]At impending slip, friction is limiting:\[G=\mu T,\qquad F=\mu S.\]Using (a):\[G+F=\mu T+\mu S\]\[=\mu\frac{40\sqrt3}4=10\sqrt3\mu.\qquad(2)\]Equate (1),(2):\[\mu=\frac1{\sqrt3}.\]

slides.title: Particles Moving on a Rough Plane

transcription.tex: We have considered motion on smooth planes and equilibrium on rough planes. Now consider motion on rough planes.\par A particle is held at rest on a rough plane inclined at \(\alpha\) to horizontal, where \(\tan\alpha=3/4\). The coefficient of friction is \(0.5\). Released, it slides downhill. Find (a) its acceleration; (b) the distance travelled in the first \(2\,\mathrm s\).

\[\tan\alpha=\frac34\]\[\Rightarrow\sin\alpha=\frac35,\quad\cos\alpha=\frac45.\]Normal to plane:\[R=mg\cos\alpha=\frac45mg.\]Down the plane:\[mg\sin\alpha-\mu R=ma\]\[\frac35mg-\frac25mg=ma\]\[a=0.2g=2.0\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\quad(2\text{ s.f.}).\]

transcription.tex: Edexcel M1 (Old), May 2013(R), Q5\par Particle \(P\), mass \(0.6\,\mathrm{kg}\), slides with constant acceleration down the line of greatest slope of a rough plane at \(25^\circ\) to horizontal. It passes \(A,B\), where \(AB=10\,\mathrm m\), taking \(3.5\,\mathrm s\) from \(A\) to \(B\). Its speed at \(A\) is \(2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find (a) its speed at \(B\); (b) its acceleration; (c) the coefficient of friction.
Normal reaction:\[R=0.6g\cos25^\circ.\]Parallel to plane:\[0.6g\sin25^\circ-\mu R=0.6a\]\[\mu=\frac{g\sin25^\circ-a}{g\cos25^\circ}\]\[=0.411\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]

transcription.tex: 7. A \(10\,\mathrm{kg}\) parcel is released from rest on a rough plane inclined at \(25^\circ\) to horizontal. (a) Find the normal reaction. After \(2\,\mathrm s\), it has moved \(4\,\mathrm m\) downhill. (b) Find the coefficient of friction.
Normal to plane:\[R-10g\cos25^\circ=0\]\[R=98\cos25^\circ=88.8\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]The normal reaction is \(88.8\,\mathrm N\).

\(u=0,s=4,t=2\); find \(a\).\[s=ut+\tfrac12at^2\]\[4=0+\tfrac12a\times2^2\quad\Rightarrow\quad a=2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}.\]Down the plane, \(F_{\rm resultant}=ma\):\[10g\sin25^\circ-\mu R=10\times2\]\[\mu\times98\cos25^\circ=10g\sin25^\circ-20\]\[\mu=\frac{98\sin25^\circ-20}{98\cos25^\circ}=0.241\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]The coefficient is \(0.24\) (2 s.f.).

transcription.tex: 8. Particle \(P\) is projected up a rough plane at angle \(\alpha\) to horizontal, where \(\tan\alpha=3/4\). The friction coefficient is \(1/3\). From \(A\), initial speed is \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); it stops momentarily at \(B\). (a) Show its uphill deceleration is \(13g/15\). Find (b) \(AB\), (c) the time from \(A\) to \(B\), both to 2 s.f.; (d) its speed on returning to \(A\).

Let mass be \(m\). Normal to plane:\[R-mg\cos\alpha=0\]\[\Rightarrow\quad R=\frac{4mg}5.\]Take uphill as positive:\[-mg\sin\alpha-\tfrac13R=ma\]\[-\frac{3mg}5-\tfrac13\frac{4mg}5=ma\]\[a=-\frac{13g}{15}.\]The deceleration is \(13g/15\).
\[v=u+at\]\[0=20-\frac{13g}{15}t\]\[t=\frac{300}{13g}=2.35\ldots\,\mathrm s\]\[t=2.4\,\mathrm s\quad(2\text{ s.f.}).\]

On moving downhill from \(B\), friction acts uphill. \(R=4mg/5\) as before. Take downhill positive:\[mg\sin\alpha-\tfrac13R=ma\]\[\frac{3mg}5-\tfrac13\frac{4mg}5=ma\]\[a=\frac g3.\]Now \(u=0,\ s=6000/(26g)\):\[v^2=u^2+2as\]\[v^2=0+\frac{2g}3\frac{6000}{26g}=\frac{4000}{26}\]\[v=12.4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]

transcription.tex: 9. A \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle is released from rest on a rough slope at angle \(\alpha\) to horizontal, where \(\tan\alpha=2/5\). After \(3\,\mathrm s\), its speed is \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find the coefficient of friction \(\mu\).

\[\tan\alpha=\frac25\Rightarrow\sin\alpha=\frac2{\sqrt{29}},\quad\cos\alpha=\frac5{\sqrt{29}}.\]\(u=0,v=6,t=3\):\[v=u+at\quad\Rightarrow\quad6=0+3a\]\[a=\frac63=2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}.\]Normal to plane:\[R=2g\cos\alpha.\]

Down the plane, \(F_{\rm resultant}=ma\):\[2g\sin\alpha-\mu R=2\times2\]\[2g\sin\alpha-\mu(2g\cos\alpha)=4\]\[g\sin\alpha-\mu g\cos\alpha=2\]\[\mu=\frac{g\sin\alpha-2}{g\cos\alpha}\]\[=\frac{9.8\times2/\sqrt{29}-2}{9.8\times5/\sqrt{29}}\]\[=0.18019\ldots.\]The coefficient of friction is \(0.180\) (3 s.f.).

transcription.tex: 11. A \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) particle is projected up a rough \(10^\circ\) slope at \(16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), stopping at \(P\) after \(5\,\mathrm s\). (a) Find \(\mu\). (b) State, with supporting calculations, whether it remains at rest or slides back downhill.

Take uphill positive. \(u=16,v=0,t=5\):\[v=u+at\quad\Rightarrow\quad0=16+5a\]\[a=-\frac{16}5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}.\]Normal to slope:\[R=5g\cos10^\circ.\]Now resolve downhill, using acceleration \(16/5\):\[5g\sin10^\circ+\mu R=5\times\frac{16}5\]\[5g\sin10^\circ+\mu\times5g\cos10^\circ=16\]\[\mu=\frac{16-5g\sin10^\circ}{5g\cos10^\circ}\]\[=0.15524\ldots.\]The coefficient is \(0.155\) (3 s.f.).

The particle slides back if the weight component downhill exceeds the maximum available friction uphill:\[5g\sin10^\circ>5\mu g\cos10^\circ\]\[\sin10^\circ>\mu\cos10^\circ\]\[0.17364\ldots>0.15288\ldots.\]This is true, so the particle slides back downhill.

transcription.tex: Connected-particle problems from Mechanics Year 1 now include friction.\par Particles \(P,Q\), masses \(5\,\mathrm{kg},10\,\mathrm{kg}\), are connected by a light inextensible string over a small smooth fixed pulley at the top of a rough plane. \(P\) rests on the plane; \(Q\) hangs freely with the string vertical and taut. The slope angle is \(\alpha\), with \(\tan\alpha=0.75\), and friction coefficient for \(P\) is \(0.2\). Released from rest, find (a) the acceleration; (b) the tension.

\[\sin\alpha=\frac35,\qquad\cos\alpha=\frac45.\]For \(P\), normal to plane:\[R=5g\cos\alpha=5g\times\frac45=4g.\]Up the plane:\[T-5g\sin\alpha-0.2R=5a\]\[T-3.8g=5a.\qquad(1)\]For \(Q\), downwards:\[10g-T=10a.\qquad(2)\]Add (1),(2):\[6.2g=15a\quad\Rightarrow\quad a=\frac{31g}{75}\]\[=4.1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\quad(2\text{ s.f.}).\]
Rearrange (1):\[T=5a+3.8g\]\[=57\,\mathrm N\quad(2\text{ s.f.}).\]Use unrounded \(a\).

transcription.tex: A light inextensible string joins block \(A\), mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\), on a smooth fixed \(30^\circ\) plane to block \(B\), mass \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\), hanging freely. It lies along the greatest slope and passes over a smooth light pulley fixed at the top. Release from rest. Model the blocks as particles and ignore air resistance. (a)(i) Show \(B\)’s acceleration is \(4g/7\); (ii) find tension. (b) How is the inextensible-string assumption used? (c) Find the magnitude of the string’s force on the pulley.
For \(A\), uphill:\[T-2g\sin30^\circ=2a\]\[T=2a+g.\qquad(1)\]For \(B\), downwards:\[5g-T=5a.\qquad(2)\]Combine (1),(2):\[5g=7a+g\quad\Rightarrow\quad a=\frac47g.\]\[T=2a+g=\frac87g+g=\frac{15}7g.\]
The taut inextensible string makes the particles’ acceleration magnitudes equal.

Tension acts away from the pulley along each string. Choose left and down as positive; factor out constant \(T\):\[\mathbf F=\begin{pmatrix}T\cos30^\circ\\T+T\sin30^\circ\end{pmatrix}\]\[=\frac T2\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt3\\3\end{pmatrix}.\]\[|\mathbf F|=\frac T2\sqrt{(\sqrt3)^2+3^2}\]\[=\frac{15}{14}g\sqrt{12}=\frac{15\sqrt3}7g\,\mathrm N.\]

transcription.tex: Edexcel M1 (Old), May 2013(R), Q3\par A rough fixed plane is inclined at \(30^\circ\) to horizontal. A small smooth pulley \(P\) is fixed at its top. Particles \(A,B\), masses \(2\,\mathrm{kg},4\,\mathrm{kg}\), are joined by a light inextensible string over \(P\). The string from \(A\) to \(P\) is parallel to the greatest slope; \(B\) hangs freely. The friction coefficient between \(A\) and the plane is \(1/\sqrt3\). Initially held at rest, release them with string taut and \(A\) moving uphill. Find the tension immediately after release. (9 marks)

For \(B\): \(4g-T=4a\).\par For \(A\): \(T-F-2g\sin30^\circ=2a\).\par Equivalently, for the whole system:\[4g-F-2g\sin30^\circ=6a.\]Normal to plane at \(A\): \(R=2g\cos30^\circ\).\[F=\mu R=\frac1{\sqrt3}\times2g\cos30^\circ=g\]\[T-g-g=T-2g=2a.\]Eliminate \(a\):\[2T-4g=4g-T\quad\Rightarrow\quad3T=8g\]\[T=\frac{8g}3=26.1\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]

transcription.tex: 3. Particles \(P,Q\), masses \(2\,\mathrm{kg},3\,\mathrm{kg}\), are connected by a light inextensible string over a small smooth fixed pulley at the top of a rough \(30^\circ\) plane. \(P\) is held at rest on the plane; \(Q\) hangs freely with string vertical and taut. On release, \(P\) accelerates uphill at \(2.5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find (a) tension; (b) the coefficient of friction; (c) the string’s force on the pulley.

For \(P\), normal to plane:\[R-2g\cos30^\circ=0\]\[\Rightarrow\quad R=g\sqrt3.\]Up the plane, \(F_{\rm resultant}=ma\):\[T-\mu R-2g\cos60^\circ=2\times2.5\]\[T-\mu g\sqrt3-g=5.\qquad(1)\]For \(Q\), downwards:\[3g-T=3\times2.5=7.5.\qquad(2)\]\[T=21.9\,\mathrm N.\]
Add (1),(2):\[2g-\mu g\sqrt3=12.5\]\[\mu g\sqrt3=7.1\]\[\mu=\frac{7.1}{g\sqrt3}=0.418\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]The coefficient is \(0.42\) (2 s.f.).
\[F=2T\cos30^\circ\]\[=43.8\cos30^\circ=37.9\,\mathrm N\quad(3\text{ s.f.}).\]The force magnitude is \(38\,\mathrm N\) (2 s.f.).

transcription.tex: 4. Particles \(A,B\), masses \(m\,\mathrm{kg},3\,\mathrm{kg}\), are connected by a light inextensible string over a smooth fixed pulley \(P\). \(A\) is held on a smooth fixed \(30^\circ\) plane, with string \(AP\) along its greatest slope; \(B\) hangs freely. Release from rest with \(B\) \(0.25\,\mathrm m\) above horizontal ground. \(B\) initially accelerates downwards at \(2g/5\). \(A\) does not reach \(P\). Find (a) tension while \(B\) descends; (b) \(m\). \(B\) hits the ground without rebounding. (c) Find the time from impact until \(A\) reaches its highest point.
For \(B\), downwards:\[3g-T=3\times\frac25g\]\[T=3g-\frac65g=\frac95g=17.64\,\mathrm N.\]The tension is \(18\,\mathrm N\) (2 s.f.).
For \(A\), uphill:\[T-mg\sin30^\circ=m\times\frac25g\]\[\frac95g-\frac12mg=\frac25mg\]\[\Rightarrow\quad m=2.\]
Before \(B\) hits the ground:\[u=0,\quad a=\frac25g,\quad s=0.25\]\[v^2=u^2+2as=\frac45g\times0.25\]\[v=1.4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.\]

After impact the string is slack, so tension is zero. The only force on \(A\) parallel to the plane is the downhill weight component. Taking uphill positive:\[-mg\sin30^\circ=ma\]\[\Rightarrow\quad a=-\frac12g.\]Now \(u=1.4,v=0\):\[v=u+at\]\[\Rightarrow\quad0=1.4-\frac12gt\]\[t=\frac{2.8}{9.8}=\frac27\,\mathrm s\]\[\approx0.29\,\mathrm s\quad(2\text{ s.f.}).\]

transcription.tex: 5. Particles \(A,B\) on back-to-back rough \(30^\circ\) slopes are connected by a light inextensible string over a smooth pulley. \(A\) has mass \(2\,\mathrm{kg}\); \(B\) has mass \(m\,\mathrm{kg}\). The friction coefficients are \(0.2\) for \(A\), \(0.4\) for \(B\). Show the maximum \(m\) before motion begins is\[\frac{10+2\sqrt3}{5-2\sqrt3}.\]

Let the reactions be \(R_A,R_B\). At maximum \(m\), impending motion is \(B\) downhill and \(A\) uphill. For \(A\):\[R_A=2g\cos30^\circ=\sqrt3g\]\[T-2g\sin30^\circ-0.2R_A=0\]\[T=g+\frac{\sqrt3}5g=\left(1+\frac{\sqrt3}5\right)g.\quad(1)\]For \(B\):\[R_B=mg\cos30^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}2mg\]\[mg\sin30^\circ-T-0.4R_B=0\]\[T=mg\left(\frac12-\frac{\sqrt3}5\right).\quad(2)\]
Equate (1),(2) and cancel \(g\):\[\left(\frac12-\frac{\sqrt3}5\right)m=1+\frac{\sqrt3}5\]\[(5-2\sqrt3)m=10+2\sqrt3\]\[m=\frac{10+2\sqrt3}{5-2\sqrt3}.\]

transcription.tex: 6. A metal block \(P\), mass \(1.5\,\mathrm{kg}\), rests on a rough horizontal workbench. A light inextensible string joins it over a small smooth pulley fixed at the edge to freely hanging box \(Q\), mass \(1.6\,\mathrm{kg}\). The coefficient of friction for \(P\) is \(\mu\). Release from rest with the string taut; after \(2\,\mathrm s\), \(Q\)’s speed is \(6\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Model both as particles. (a) Find acceleration of \(Q\); (b) tension; (c) show \(\mu=0.434\) (3 s.f.); (d) how is inextensibility used?
\[v=u+at\quad\Rightarrow\quad6=0+2a\]\[a=\frac62=3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}.\]
For \(Q\), Newton’s second law:\[1.6g-T=1.6\times3\]\[T=1.6g-1.6\times3\]\[=1.6(9.8-3)=10.88\,\mathrm N.\]The tension is \(10.88\,\mathrm N\).
The taut inextensible string gives both particles equal acceleration magnitudes. Equal tension follows from the light string and smooth pulley.
